case.presentation: An 82-year-old male with a history of HTN, HLD, CAD, CKD, and prostate cancer metastasized to the lungs presents with acute onset pain, stiffness, swelling, and redness of the hands and feet. Symptoms began with pain and progressed to stiffness, swelling, and tenderness by the 5th day. He was recently started on pantoprazole but symptoms began before that. He is taking capecitabine daily and receiving oxaliplatin infusions every three weeks for chemotherapy. On exam, he has swelling of his digits, significant cracking and dry skin, particularly on the toes and plantar foot, and pink coloration of the palms and soles. Should I start oral prednisone?
case.recommendations: Favor hand-foot syndrome (acral erythema/palmoplantar erythrodysesthesia) given the history. This condition is often associated with systemic chemotherapeutic agents like capecitabine. Treatment includes halobetasol 0.05% ointment BID for 2-4 weeks for symptomatic relief, along with a petrolatum-based moisturizer applied to affected areas generously. Systemic steroids are generally not recommended. Removing the offending agent may resolve the condition if it is indeed hand-foot syndrome. If it is palmoplantar keratoderma due to underlying malignancy, treatment would be symptomatic or addressing the malignancy. Patient should report worsening skin breakdown or fever. Significant improvement is expected in 2-4 weeks, with potential for future flares if the culprit drug is re-administered. If there is no improvement or worsening, an in-person exam can be arranged.
